messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 73
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: North American
- Relationship Status: Divorced
- Occupation: Journalist
- Trauma Type: Man-made disaster
- Pcl5: 74

He is 73 now, a North American man who has spent most of his adult life working as a journalist, the kind who once believed that bearing witness was a form of service. For decades he learned to stand close to chaos without flinching. He prides himself on noticing details other people miss: the scorch mark on a wall, the tremor in a mayor’s hand, the silence after a question no one wants to answer. He says that before the disaster, this ability felt like a professional gift. Afterward, it begins to feel more like a trap.

The event happens late in his career, when he is sent to cover an industrial explosion at a chemical plant on the edge of a midsized city. At first he approaches it as he has approached every breaking story: notebook in pocket, recorder in hand, mind already shaping headlines. The sky above the plant is streaked with black smoke. Sirens overlap. People run in directions that make no sense. He remembers the smell most vividly, a sharp, metallic burn that catches in his throat and makes his eyes water. He moves closer than he should. He tells himself he needs to see for himself.

Then a second blast throws debris across the lot and knocks him to the ground. For a few seconds he cannot hear anything but a high ringing. When he looks up, a man near the chain-link fence is on fire. Another worker is screaming for his brother. There are pieces of concrete, twisted metal, and something he knows is part of a body before his mind can fully name it. He crawls behind a news van, stunned and ashamed at how quickly his training disappears. Later he cannot remember how he gets out, only that he does, and that he keeps his notebook clenched in his fist so hard the spiral binding cuts into his palm.

In the days that follow, he files his story. He writes clean copy under deadline and accepts colleagues’ praise for staying composed. He does not feel composed. He feels split in two: the public version of himself, dry-eyed and articulate, and the private one who startles at the hiss of the radiator and smells chemicals in his clothes long after they have been washed. At night he sees the burning man the moment he closes his eyes. Sometimes the dream is exact; sometimes it changes and he is the one trapped behind the fence, unable to breathe, calling out while no one comes. He wakes drenched in sweat, disoriented, his heart pounding hard enough that he sits on the side of the bed and checks whether he is having a heart attack.

Over the next months, his world narrows. He stops driving near the industrial district. He turns down assignments involving fires, explosions, or large crowds, then begins inventing reasons to avoid the newsroom altogether. He tells former coworkers he prefers freelancing from home, but at home he spends long periods staring at a blank screen. When an editor asks for a retrospective on the anniversary of the explosion, he agrees automatically and then becomes so agitated researching it that he throws up in his kitchen sink. He is humiliated by the force of his reaction. He has spent a lifetime interviewing grieving families and disaster survivors; he cannot reconcile that history with the fact that now a photograph of a smoke plume can leave him shaky for hours.

His ex-wife says he has become harder, though they have been divorced for years and mostly speak by phone. He snaps at her when she asks simple questions. He rarely answers calls from his adult children on the first try because the sudden ring makes him jump. He used to meet other retired reporters for coffee and gossip; now he finds excuses to stay away because restaurants feel exposed and noisy. If a plate shatters or a truck backfires outside, his whole body reacts before he can think. He scans exits, watches people’s hands, and sits only where he can see the door. He hates this vigilance and relies on it.

What troubles him most is the guilt. He circles the same thoughts repeatedly: he should not have gone closer; he should have helped someone; he should not have made a career out of witnessing other people’s catastrophe. He remembers writing down descriptions while workers searched for the missing, and the memory fills him with disgust. He calls himself a vulture, though he also knows his reporting exposed negligence at the plant and mattered to the city. Both things seem true to him, and he cannot settle the contradiction.

In the present, his apartment is quiet, almost carefully so. He keeps the television volume low and avoids live news unless he has prepared himself. He sleeps in short stretches. Some mornings he wakes already exhausted, as if he has spent the night outrunning something. He still writes, but more slowly, and often abandons pieces when they come too close to danger or loss. He says he does not feel like the man he was before the explosion. The world no longer seems accidental or orderly; it seems primed for rupture. Even in calm moments, he waits for the next blast.
